title: Sugar
subtitle: 8000–1200 BC · Sweetness Before Sugar: Honey and Dates, and the Reed Domesticated in New Guinea

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: A honey gatherer on the wall of a Spanish shelter and a beekeeper carved in Egypt

entries.label: The honey gatherer of Bicorp
entries.hint: In a rock shelter of the Coves de l’Aranya, a Levantine-art painting shows a figure climbing to a hive in a crevice to take honey — one of the oldest images of honey hunting. Its age is disputed, estimated at anywhere from 8000 to 6000 BC, and recent work questions both the dating and the sex of the climber.
entries.note: CONTESTED DATE (secondary): Wikipedia, ‘Cuevas de la Araña’ (about 8,000 years, epipalaeolithic, ‘dating of such art is controversial’); El Temps (7,500 years); Honeybee Histories (Neolithic, about 6,000 years); Kritsky, American Bee Journal 160(11), 2020, who notes that questions about the age and the sex of the honey hunter are challenging earlier interpretations. The rope-ladder detail often attached to the scene belongs to the nearby Barranco Gómez painting at Castellote, not to Bicorp.

entries.label: Niuserre’s sun temple shows the first beekeeper
entries.hint: In the Room of the Seasons of Niuserre’s sun temple a relief shows a beekeeper with horizontal hives — smoke to quiet the bees, combs taken out, the honey strained and sealed in jars — the earliest known picture of beekeeping and proof that honey was already a managed, stored product in Old Kingdom Egypt.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular and encyclopaedic summaries; the UCL Digital Egypt page could not be fetched): the relief is described as the earliest known depiction of beekeeping, in the Room of the Seasons, now in the Egyptian Museum, Berlin; Niuserre’s reign is given as 2445–2421 BC. The scholarly source to check is Kritsky, The Tears of Ra (2015). A second bee scene from the Unas causeway was reported in the 1930s. See egypt-3000bc-2100bc::b3.
keywords: Room of the Seasons of Niuserre

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The reconstructed Austronesian word for sugarcane

entries.label: A reconstructed word for sugarcane in Proto-Austronesian
entries.hint: Sugarcane has a reconstructed name in Proto-Austronesian (*təbuS or *CebuS), continued as *tebuh in Proto-Malayo-Polynesian and *topu in Proto-Oceanic — evidence that it was a named crop of the Austronesian speakers who spread out from Taiwan, and one of their original major crops according to one summary.
entries.note: SECONDARY (the cognate set itself was not retrieved): Blust (1984–85) and later work as summarised in Wikipedia ‘Sugarcane’ (the ‘at least 5,500 BP’ antiquity is that article’s, with its footnotes to Blust and Spriggs 2011); Proto-Oceanic *topu from Ross, Pawley & Osmond’s lexicon, via a search summary; the Austronesian Comparative Dictionary online lists reflexes such as Berawan təppuh ‘sugarcane’ (Blust 1971). The reconstructed word names a plant, not a sugar.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: New Guinea’s early gardens, Neolithic beeswax, the date palm and the first cane in the archaeological record

entries.label: Kuk Swamp: the early agriculture of New Guinea
entries.loc: Kuk Swamp, Wahgi valley, Western Highlands
entries.hint: At Kuk Swamp in the New Guinea Highlands, drained and dug wetland plots show cultivation beginning perhaps 10,000 years ago on Golson and Hughes’s reading, or around 6950–6440 years ago on Denham’s. Whichever is right, it is the agricultural landscape in which sugarcane was domesticated. Sugarcane itself is not attested at Kuk in the chapter read for this folio.
entries.note: ANCHOR (chapter read): Denham, Golson & Hughes, ‘Phase 1: The case for 10,000-year-old agriculture at Kuk’, ch.11 in Golson et al. (eds), Ten Thousand Years of Cultivation at Kuk Swamp in the Highlands of Papua New Guinea (ANU Press, 2017) — the chapter text does not mention sugarcane or Saccharum. The Denham date 6950–6440 cal BP comes from a search summary of Denham’s 2004 paper and should be checked. Wikipedia’s statement that cane and bananas were cultivated at Kuk 6900–6400 BP is not supported by this chapter.

entries.label: Beeswax in Neolithic cooking pots
entries.hint: Lipid analysis of Neolithic pottery shows that early farmers used honeybee products: the oldest beeswax residues come from cooking pots in Turkey of the seventh millennium BC, and the signature turns up at many European sites. The residues show exploitation of wax and honey, not necessarily beekeeping — honey was the sweetener that sugar would later replace.
entries.note: SECONDARY (the Nature page was not readable; press and news summaries read): Roffet-Salque et al., ‘Widespread exploitation of the honeybee by early Neolithic farmers’, Nature 527 (2015) pp.226ff, via the Bristol press release, Chemistry World and public-radio summaries (more than 6,000 sherds from more than 150 sites; only about 100 vessels carried the beeswax signature). One news report names the Turkish site as Çatalhöyük — unverified.

entries.label: The date palm, sweet crop of the Gulf and the Mesopotamian south
entries.hint: In the Gulf and southern Mesopotamia the date palm was the sweet crop: charred stones from Dalma island, c.5000–4500 BC, are among the earliest evidence for eating dates, and the palm — which also gave wood and fibre — grew between the fields of the Ubaid south. For millennia dates and honey, not cane, were the sweet things of the Near East.
entries.note: CONTEXT: the sourcing is in gulf-prehistory-8000bc-3000bc::ec4 (Dalma) and mesopotamia-6500bc-3800bc::e2, whose entries describe the date palm as sugar-rich and a source of ‘sugar, wood, fibre and shade’. No cane or refined sugar is attested in the Near East in this period.

entries.label: The first sugarcane in the archaeological record
entries.hint: Sugarcane enters the world archaeological record about 2500 BC in New Guinea — the only archaeological find known when Needham surveyed the question — although the plant was probably in use far earlier, since Golson has evidence for agriculture in New Guinea as early as 7000 BC.
entries.note: SECONDARY (the find itself was not checked): Needham, Science and Civilisation in China 6.3 (Daniels & Menzies 1996) p.129 and n.b, citing Bulmer (1) pp.29–33 and Golson (2) p.46. Needham notes that the find appeared ‘about the time of the earliest datings for rice’.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The domestication of sugarcane from wild robustum cane

entries.label: Sugarcane is domesticated from wild robustum cane
entries.loc: New Guinea and the islands east of the Wallace line
entries.hint: Sugarcane (Saccharum officinarum) was domesticated in New Guinea and nearby islands from the wild cane S. robustum, by selecting plants with sugar-rich pith that could be chewed. Genomic work dates it to about 8,000 years ago (c.6000 BC) and finds the cultivated genome a mosaic of different robustum subgroups; older models put the first spread from New Guinea as early as 8000 BC. In Denham’s reconstruction, people first managed and moved wild robustum, then selected the sweet plants, before the dispersal.
entries.note: ANCHOR (press release and abstract read; the Cell paper itself was not retrieved): Garsmeur et al., ‘The genomic footprints of wild Saccharum species trace domestication, diversification, and modern breeding of sugarcane’, Cell (2025), doi 10.1016/j.cell.2025.09.017, as reported in the CIRAD press release of October 2025 (390 accessions; domestication ‘around 8,000 years ago’); Denham, ‘Forgetting cane grasses: switching temporal focus to reveal mosaics of Saccharum diversity’, Plants People Planet 7(3) (2025) pp.590–602, doi 10.1002/ppp3.10489 (abstract read; it gives no dates); Mintz, Sweetness and Power (1985) p.19 (Artschwager & Brandes: first diffusion c.8000 BC); Needham SCC 6.3 p.130 (S. officinarum evolved in New Guinea and the islands east of the Wallace line); Buttery (2022) p.6 (c.8000 BCE). The sources differ by about two thousand years on the date.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The older diffusion model and the voyagers who carried cane through the Pacific

entries.label: Brandes’s three diffusions: an older model
entries.loc: New Guinea to the Philippines and India
entries.hint: The botanists Artschwager and Brandes proposed three diffusions of cane from New Guinea: the first around 8000 BC, a second perhaps two thousand years later to the Philippines and India and possibly Indonesia. It was the standard account for decades, but the 2025 genomic study ties the continental-Asian centre of diversification to human movements only about 3,000 years ago.
entries.note: CONTESTED: Mintz (1985) p.19 citing Artschwager & Brandes (1958) (some authorities treat Indonesia as another locus of domestication); Buttery (2022) p.6 (cane in India and China ‘around 6000 BCE’); Kieschnick (2003) p.250 n.104; Needham SCC 6.3 p.130 (S. sinense developed in south China, best guess Yunnan; S. barberi in north India — as hybrids with wild S. spontaneum). The genomic dating is treated in the Ancient sugar folio.

entries.label: The voyagers carry cane through the island Pacific
entries.hint: Sugarcane was carried into the Melanesian and Polynesian islands by migrating peoples between about 3,500 and 500 years ago, where it hybridised with a previously unknown wild ancestor — probably from eastern Melanesia — and with Miscanthus; this island centre of diversification shaped most modern cane varieties.
entries.note: ANCHOR (press release read): CIRAD press release (October 2025) on Garsmeur et al. — introduction ‘between 3,500 and 500 years ago’, hybridisation with an unknown ancestor ‘probably originating from eastern Melanesia’ and with Miscanthus; Buttery (2022) p.6 (Hawaii in the first millennium AD, via Vaughan & Geissler 2009 p.18). Whether Lapita voyagers carried cane was not checked.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The wild canes of Asia and New Guinea; the northern limit of the honeybee

entries.label: The wild canes: robustum, spontaneum and edule
entries.hint: Two wild species frame the story: Saccharum robustum on New Guinea and the Indonesian islands east of the Wallace line, ancestor of the sweet cane, and S. spontaneum, ranging from the Mediterranean through Asia to its eastern edge, the partner in the later hybrids. A third form, S. edule, is cultivated for its edible flower-head.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Needham SCC 6.3 p.129 n.g (citing Daniels & Roach (1) tables 6–7, pp.26, 29); Grivet et al. 2004 and Denham 2025 for the ancestry (abstract only). The date is a placeholder for the pre-domestication baseline.

entries.label: The honeybee’s northern limit at the 57th parallel
entries.hint: The Neolithic pottery survey found no beeswax at sites north of the 57th parallel (Scotland, Fennoscandia), which the authors read as the northern limit of the honeybee in the early Neolithic.
entries.note: SECONDARY (summaries read, not the paper): Roffet-Salque et al., Nature 527 (2015), via the Bristol and Exeter press releases and public-radio coverage.
